stops.title: Uruk, the first big city
stops.blurb: By about 3300 BCE, Uruk in southern Mesopotamia had grown into something new: a city of tens of thousands of people, most of whom did not grow their own food. It had huge temple buildings, mass-produced pottery, and officials who kept track of grain, sheep and labour. Its goods and styles turn up from Iran to Syria and Anatolia.

stops.title: Writing begins as bookkeeping
stops.blurb: The first writing was accounting. Around 3300 BCE, Uruk's administrators pressed signs into clay tablets to record grain, beer, cloth and livestock. Over the next centuries the signs came to stand for sounds, so they could record names, laws, letters and stories. Egyptian hieroglyphs appeared at almost the same time. Writing was later invented from scratch in China and in Mesoamerica.
stops.dateNote: The oldest tablets from Uruk are dated to roughly 3350 to 3200 BCE.

stops.title: Herders from the steppe
stops.blurb: Around 3300 BCE the Yamnaya herders appeared on the grasslands north of the Black and Caspian Seas, and by 3000 BCE they ranged from Hungary to Kazakhstan. About 4,500 years ago, people in central Europe traced roughly three-quarters of their ancestry to them. Ancient DNA suggests these migrations carried at least some of Europe's Indo-European languages, though where that language family first arose is still argued over.
stops.debate: Where and when the Indo-European languages began. Ancient DNA supports a spread from the steppe into Europe; a 2023 study of vocabulary dates the family's root to about 8,100 years ago, earlier than the steppe migrations.
stops.dateNote: The Yamnaya culture appeared around 3300 BCE. This stop starts at 3000 BCE, when it reached its widest extent.

stops.title: The planned cities of the Indus
stops.blurb: From about 2600 BCE, cities rose along the Indus and neighbouring rivers in what is now Pakistan and northwest India. Mohenjo-daro and Harappa were laid out in an orderly plan, with baked-brick houses, wells, bathing rooms and covered drains. Their people traded by sea with Mesopotamia and used a script nobody has deciphered. After about 1900 BCE the cities emptied, probably as the monsoon weakened.

stops.title: Caral: cities on the far side of the world
stops.blurb: While pyramids were rising in Egypt, people on the desert coast of Peru were raising their own. Caral, occupied from about 2600 to 2000 BCE, had six large platform mounds and sunken circular plazas, fed by irrigated fields. Its builders had no pottery and no writing, and no contact with any other city-builders. Cities were invented more than once.

stops.title: The Great Pyramid, and the last mammoths
stops.blurb: Around 2560 BCE, Egypt's king Khufu had the Great Pyramid built at Giza. Papyrus logbooks found at a Red Sea harbour, the oldest inscribed papyri known, record a work crew ferrying limestone blocks to the site. Far to the north, a small herd of woolly mammoths was still alive on Wrangel Island in the Arctic. They died out about 4,000 years ago.

stops.title: Kerma, a Nubian kingdom on the Nile
stops.blurb: Around 2500 BCE, at the northern end of the Great Bend of the Nile in what is now Sudan, Nubians founded Kerma, the earliest city in Africa outside Egypt. Its kings came to rule much of the Nile valley south of Egypt and were buried in vast tombs with hundreds of sacrifices. Kerma traded and fought with Egypt for centuries, until Egyptian armies conquered it around 1450 BCE.

stops.title: The first empire, and the first author we can name
stops.blurb: Around 2340 BCE Sargon of Akkad conquered the city-states of Sumer and joined peoples of different languages and gods under one ruler: the first empire. He made his daughter Enheduanna high priestess of the moon god at Ur. She wrote hymns in Sumerian and named herself in them, "I, Enheduanna", which makes her the earliest author we know by name.

stops.title: Hammurabi's laws in stone
stops.blurb: Hammurabi, king of Babylon from 1792 to 1750 BCE, had his laws carved on a basalt pillar more than two metres tall, topped by a relief of the king before the sun god Shamash. He wrote that they were meant so "the strong should not harm the weak". Punishments depended on rank: putting out a man's eye cost an eye, but a slave's eye cost half the slave's value.

stops.title: Lapita voyagers sail into the open Pacific
stops.blurb: Between about 1500 and 1300 BCE a new style of pottery, called Lapita, appeared in the Bismarck Archipelago off New Guinea. Within two or three centuries its makers sailed east into the open Pacific, reaching Vanuatu, then Fiji, then Tonga around 890 BCE, islands where no one had lived before. Ancient DNA shows that the first settlers of Vanuatu had little or no Papuan ancestry.

stops.title: Bronze, tin and the Uluburun ship
stops.blurb: Around 1320 BCE a merchant ship sank off Uluburun on the coast of Turkey. It carried 10 tonnes of copper ingots from Cyprus and a tonne of tin, the two metals that make bronze. Tin is far rarer than copper. Chemical tests show that a third of the ship's tin came from ores in today's Uzbekistan and Tajikistan, and the rest from Turkey's Taurus Mountains.

stops.title: Shang China and the oracle bones
stops.blurb: The oldest Chinese writing known is carved on oracle bones: ox shoulder blades and turtle shells used for divination by the kings of the late Shang dynasty. Over 150,000 have been found, most at Yinxu near Anyang, the late Shang capital. Until 1899 farmers sold them as "dragon bones" for medicine. Radiocarbon dates put King Wu Ding's reign at about 1254 to 1197 BCE.
stops.dateNote: The dates span the late Shang, from Wu Ding's reign to the dynasty's end around 1041 BCE, as estimated from radiocarbon dates on the bones.

stops.title: The Bronze Age world falls apart
stops.blurb: Within about fifty years of 1200 BCE, the connected world of the eastern Mediterranean came apart. The Hittite empire vanished, the Mycenaean palaces burned, the trading city of Ugarit was destroyed and never rebuilt, and Egypt lost its lands abroad. Historians point to drought, earthquakes, migration and war, and to how much these states had come to depend on one another.
stops.debate: No single cause is agreed. Knapp and Manning argue for many local crises over decades; others give more weight to a long drought.

p: Around 3300 BCE, officials in Uruk began marking clay tablets with signs for things and numbers. A typical tablet records amounts of barley, beer, cloth, sheep or workers, and who was responsible for them. This system is called proto-cuneiform. It could not yet record a sentence: it was a tool for keeping accounts in an economy too large for memory. Over the following centuries, scribes began using signs for their sounds as well as their meanings. That let them spell names and, eventually, write down speech. The wedge-shaped script that grew out of it, cuneiform, was used for about 3,000 years and for more than a dozen languages.

Excavators at Uruk recovered around five thousand of these early tablets, most of them thrown out as rubbish in ancient times and reused as building fill. The great majority are administrative records. The rest are lists of words, such as names of professions, animals and vessels, which scribes copied to learn the signs. Because the tablets are clay, they survived; records kept on wood, cloth or string elsewhere mostly did not.

Scholars disagree about what came before the tablets. One view holds that small clay tokens, used for counting across the region for thousands of years, developed step by step into written signs. Others see the tokens as only one of several sources. It is also unsettled whether Egyptians invented their hieroglyphs independently or borrowed the idea of writing from Mesopotamia; the earliest Egyptian labels are about as old as the Uruk tablets. Writing in China and in Mesoamerica is agreed to have been invented separately.

Writing let knowledge outlive the people who held it and travel further than anyone could carry it in memory. Laws, contracts, letters, astronomy, medicine and literature all followed. It also marks a boundary in how we know the past: before writing, we have only objects and bones, and after it, we begin to have names and voices. That it began with accounts says something about what the first cities needed most.

Around 3300 BCE a new archaeological culture, the Yamnaya, appeared on the steppes north of the Black and Caspian Seas. By 3000 BCE it stretched from Hungary in the west to Kazakhstan in the east. Its people were herders. Ancient DNA shows that about four-fifths of their ancestry came from people who had lived between the Caucasus and the lower Volga, and the rest from hunter-gatherers of eastern Europe.

About 4,500 years ago the effects reached the heart of Europe. People of the Corded Ware culture in what is now Germany traced about three-quarters of their ancestry to the Yamnaya. This was a large migration, not only the spread of new goods or ideas, and steppe ancestry is still found in present-day Europeans.

The evidence comes from ancient genomes. In 2015 one team read DNA from 69 people who lived in Europe between 8,000 and 3,000 years ago and traced how its populations mixed and replaced one another. A 2025 study added 435 people from the steppe and the lands around it to find where the Yamnaya's own ancestors came from.

Languages leave no bones, so linking a language to a migration is an inference. Genetics shows where people moved and when. Linguists compare core vocabulary across the Indo-European languages to estimate when and where their common ancestor was spoken.

Where the Indo-European languages began is one of the longest-running arguments about the past. One view holds that they spread with horse-using herders from the steppe about 6,000 years ago; another, that they spread with the first farmers out of Anatolia about 9,000 years ago. A 2023 study of core vocabulary dated the family's root to about 8,100 years ago, too early for the steppe view. It proposed a homeland south of the Caucasus, with a later branch that moved north onto the steppe and then across Europe.

The 2025 DNA study proposes instead that the shared ancestor of Hittite and the other Indo-European languages was spoken by the people between the Caucasus and the lower Volga, some time between 4400 and 4000 BCE. Both views accept that the steppe migrations carried at least some Indo-European languages into Europe.

Within a few centuries the steppe migrations reshaped the ancestry of a continent. They are also a clear case of ancient DNA changing an old argument: a question once argued only from words and pottery can now be tested against the genomes of the people themselves.

Before about 2350 BCE, southern Mesopotamia was divided among Sumerian city-states. Each was ruled by a king and centred on the temple of its own god: Ur belonged to Nanna, the moon god, and Uruk to Inanna, goddess of love and war. Later legend says Sargon began as a cupbearer at the court of Kish. He overthrew its king, built a kingdom in the north, then defeated Lugalzagesi of Umma, who had conquered much of Sumer, and united all of Mesopotamia.

Sargon sent Akkadian governors to the Sumerian cities and made Akkadian the official language. Administrative documents say he kept a force of 5,400 men. The Sumerian cities revolted at least twice and were crushed. The empire grew under his grandson Naram-Sin and broke apart after the death of his great-grandson Sharkalisharri.
Sargon made his daughter Enheduanna high priestess of Nanna at Ur. Her first language was probably Akkadian, but she wrote in Sumerian, the language of the south.

In 1927 the archaeologist Leonard Woolley found an alabaster disk at Ur. On it a woman, larger than the figures around her, leads a ceremony at an altar. The inscription names her as Enheduanna, priestess of the moon god and daughter of Sargon. About 8,000 clay tablets from the period, royal inscriptions and everyday records of trade and law, show how the empire was run.

Enheduanna's songs survive in later copies. About 100 tablets carry one of them, all written after her death. In two songs to Inanna she speaks in her own voice: "I, En-hedu-ana, will recite a prayer to you."

How Sargon built and held his empire is still unclear. Assyriologists do not know whether it grew from a plan or from a run of opportunities. Enheduanna's poems are some of the hardest Sumerian texts to translate. They use words found nowhere else, and Sumerian has no living relative to compare it with, so readings of them differ.

Sargon's empire was the first state to bring several peoples, languages and city-states under one ruler. Later kings, Hammurabi of Babylon among them, modelled their reigns on the Akkadian rulers. Enheduanna is the earliest author whose name we know, and the only author in Mesopotamian history of whom a portrait made in her lifetime survives.
